Neonates of the Giant chimaera emerge at approximately 16.4 cm [Lb = approximately 16.4 cm] in total length, a value inferred from the closely related Chimaera monstrosa and consistent with the relatively large offspring size that characterizes holocephalans. This substantial length at birth reflects a prolonged yolk-dependent embryonic phase, during which the developing young attain a well-developed body plan prior to parturition. Field surveys of ovigerous tracts in congeneric species indicate that the pups are fully formed upon emergence, exhibiting the dorsal fin spine and characteristic morphological features of the genus. The size at birth among chimaeroids is generally conservative, with this value falling within the range documented for other members of the family Chimaeridae. Such a life-history strategy, wherein a single large offspring is produced per oviductal capsule, minimizes early postnatal mortality risks by reducing the duration of vulnerability to predation during the earliest stages of independent existence.

A comprehensive analysis of growth trajectories for Chimaera lignaria reveals that this species attains a maximum or ultimate total length of 142 cm [Li = 142 cm], a figure representing the largest size recorded among reliably measured adult specimens. This asymptotic dimension positions the Giant chimaera as one of the more sizable members of its genus, exceeding the typical lengths reported for C. monstrosa and C. phantasma in comparable studies. Size at full somatic maturity is seldom achieved before several decades of life, given the slow growth and extended generation times typical of deep-water chondrichthyans. The ultimate length is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 18,700 grams [Wwi = 18,700 grams], derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a robust sample of individuals spanning the full adult size range. This body mass, attained only by the largest reproductively active adults, places the species at the upper end of the biomass spectrum for holocephalans inhabiting similar bathyal environments.

Sexual maturation in this species follows distinct trajectories between the sexes, with females reaching puberty at a significantly larger body size than males. The total length at puberty for females has been estimated at 88.6 cm [Lp = 88.6 cm], representing the threshold at which ovarian development and vitellogenesis are first initiated under sustained natural conditions. Males, by contrast, attain puberty at a total length of 65.9 cm [Lp = 65.9 cm], a value that corresponds to a markedly earlier life stage and a lower somatic investment prior to reproductive activation. This pattern of sexual size dimorphism at maturation, with females exceeding males by more than 20 cm, is commonly observed in elasmobranchs and chimaeroids and is thought to reflect the greater energetic demands of gestation and egg capsule production. Examination of the clasper calcification and testicular tissue confirms that functional maturity in males is achieved at the smaller length, whereas females require additional years of somatic growth before their first reproductive event becomes feasible.

Life-history timing in the Giant chimaera is strongly modulated by the prevailing water temperature at depth, which in the species' preferred habitat remains near 3.6 °C [T = 3.6 °C]. Under this thermal regime, the maximum reproductive rate has been quantified as a single egg capsule containing one pup per reproductive event [N_R_i = one pup per reproductive event], with approximately 6 such events per year [F_R_i = approximately 6 such events per year]. This low fecundity is characteristic of chondrichthyans occupying cold, oligotrophic ecosystems where metabolic constraints limit both growth rates and reproductive investment. At the same ambient temperature of 3.6 °C [T = 3.6 °C], the maximum lifespan for this species is estimated at approximately 43 years [am = approximately 43 years], a longevity that ranks among the highest documented for any holocephalan and reflects the exceptionally slow pace of life in deep, thermally stable waters. Such extreme lifespans are consistent with the extremely low mortality rates and slow metabolic processes typical of abyssal organisms.

The temporal framework of sexual development under these cold conditions reveals a pronounced difference between the sexes. Females require approximately 33 years since birth [tp = approximately 33 years since birth] to reach sexual maturity, whereas males reach puberty in roughly 17 years since birth [tp = roughly 17 years since birth], both values recorded at the same habitat temperature of 3.6 °C [T = 3.6 °C]. This substantial delay in female maturation, nearly double that of males, aligns with the disparity in body size at puberty and underscores the energetic premium placed on attaining sufficient somatic mass to support egg production. The cold thermal environment effectively extends all developmental intervals relative to warmer-water chimaerids, making this species one of the slowest-maturing vertebrates known. These life-history parameters, when combined with the low fecundity and great longevity, paint a picture of an organism whose demographic strategy is heavily skewed toward persistence rather than rapid turnover.

Given the extreme depths at which the Giant chimaera resides, observations of live individuals in their natural habitat remain rare, and much of the current knowledge on its life history derives from bycatch records and morphological analyses of preserved specimens. Studies of the digestive tract suggest a diet dominated by benthic invertebrates such as crustaceans, mollusks, and echinoderms, which are abundant in the bathyal zone. The slow metabolic rate imposed by the persistently cold environment at 3.6 °C likely influences not only growth and reproduction but also the frequency of feeding events and the efficiency of nutrient assimilation. Comparative research on deep-sea chondrichthyans indicates that species adapted to such thermally stable yet resource-limited settings tend to exhibit low activity levels and reduced metabolic demands, further reinforcing the pattern of delayed maturation and extended longevity documented here. Ongoing monitoring of population age structure using vertebral banding patterns may provide additional insights into the demographic resilience of this enigmatic holocephalan.
